L’asphyxie du communautaire freine la pr: Community sector suffocation is holding back crime prevention in Montréal
Comment le sous-financement chronique de: How chronic underfunding of Montréal’s community organizations is weakening youth crime prevention.
Un des combats lors du gala organisé par: One of the bouts at the gala organized by Ness Martial to raise funds. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
La réalisation de cet article s’inscrit: This article was produced amid a mobilization of the community sector, as organizations across Quebec take part in the strike movement Le communautaire à boutte. We chose to look at youth crime prevention, a particularly sensitive field of intervention that people working on the ground often describe as one of the most urgent.
Notre démarche s’est fondée sur des obse: Our approach was based on field observations and interviews with youth workers, young people and community stakeholders, notably in Saint-Michel and Côte-des-Neiges. Some of the figures cited, such as the number of projects rejected under the Programme québécois de lutte contre la criminalité, come from exchanges between organizations at a meeting of the Comité de prévention urbaine (CPU) and have not been the subject of detailed official publications. The Ministère de la Sécurité publique was contacted but did not comment specifically on the situations described, referring us instead to the program’s official criteria.
Le contexte actuel, marqué par l’instabi: The current context, marked by instability and mobilization in the sector, is an integral part of the reality documented in this article.
<strong>Dans des quartiers de Montréal o: In Montréal neighbourhoods where violence and school dropout remain persistent issues, several delinquency prevention organizations have had their funding requests rejected under the Programme québécois de lutte contre la criminalité. In Saint-Michel, for example, out of about ten projects submitted locally, only one was approved, and only partially funded. On the ground, the consequences of this instability are already being felt: services are suspended, activities are cancelled, youth workers are leaving. And, in the void left behind, young people find themselves without supervision in neighbourhoods that are already vulnerable.
Dans la grande salle de la maison des je: In the main hall of the Chalet Kent youth centre in Côte-des-Neiges, about thirty teenagers shout, laugh and call out to one another in an almost deafening racket. “Simon says!”, or rather “Fabou says!”, a reworked version of the game, rattles off one instruction after another. Bodies are moving, voices are rising, bursts of laughter ring out.
Dans un coin, d’autres regardent un matc: In one corner, others are watching a soccer game. Some are chatting, sitting in armchairs. Here, time stretches differently. “It’s a place for young people. You feel comfortable here, it’s better than home,” sums up Youcef, 15, who has been coming for five years. “We talk with the others, we play… and, you know, we’re safe.”
À quelques mètres, l’animateur Mohamed-H: A few metres away, youth leader Mohamed-Hazer Berhouma keeps an eye on the room while talking with a group. He describes his role simply: “We listen to them, we help them… sometimes, some of them tell us about situations related to crime.” Then he sums up what is at stake: “If they don’t come here, they go out on the street.” That afternoon, he has planned an activity involving rewards. They are snacks and small gift cards that, for that matter, will be paid for by him and his colleague. “We even give from our own pockets, so that they stay here, so that they spend less time on the street.”
La Maison des jeunes n’est pas qu’un lie: The youth centre is not just a place for recreation. It is a pivotal space between school and home. “We’re here to fill that void,” explains coordinator Marilia Beltrame. “Parents often work late. Kids get out of school at 4 p.m.… and there are still hours to fill.”
Dans ce quartier parmi les plus multieth: In this neighbourhood, one of the most multiethnic in Montréal, many families are newly arrived. Their bearings are still being built. “There’s a bit of everything here,” the coordinator notes. “People who are well settled, others who are just starting their lives in Canada. And that creates different needs.”
Pour y répondre, la maison des jeunes fo: To meet them, the youth centre operates on a “drop-in” basis: an open space where teenagers can come in freely, play, talk or simply be there.
Mais derrière cette apparente simplicité: But behind this apparent simplicity, the machinery is fragile. “We’re short on staff. Everywhere,” Marilia says. “The needs are clear: to supervise about thirty young people, two youth workers are legally required. Ideally three, because in the summer we can have up to 60 kids… and sometimes there are only two of us.”
Les projets permettent d’embaucher des t: Projects make it possible to hire temporary workers. As soon as they end, the positions disappear. “We train young people, we hire them… then we can’t keep them.” The result: constant staff turnover, which weakens the bonds with the teenagers. “We’ve had incredible youth workers. They leave because the pay is better elsewhere.” Salaries, meanwhile, stagnate. “We’re not competitive,” she admits.
À quelques kilomètres de là, à Saint-Mic: A few kilometres away, in Saint-Michel, the situation is even more precarious. Mohamed Mimoun, director of the Forum jeunesse, does not mince words: “We’ve reached the point where we risk no longer being able to pay for our space.”
Son organisme accueille des jeunes que d: His organization welcomes young people whom others turn away: “Those with behavioural problems, those who have no place left anywhere else.” But without funding, services are shrinking. “We lost our only youth worker. He found another job.”
Conséquence immédiate : une activité heb: The immediate consequences: a weekly cooking activity cancelled, a youth radio project stopped, a space open only intermittently: “When I’m here, they’re here. When I’m not here… there’s no one.”
Ce qui inquiète le plus Mohamed Mimoun,: What worries Mohamed Mimoun most is not only the loss of services, but what is happening outside. “If we close too much, the kids will go elsewhere. And that elsewhere scares us.” In his work, he observes warning signs: boredom, lack of opportunities, economic pressure starting at age 13 or 14. “A kid tells me, ‘I want to work.’ But he doesn’t have the networks, doesn’t have the skills… and sometimes, there’s discrimination.” Two factors then become decisive: the prospect of success and a sense of belonging. “If he doesn’t have that, he becomes vulnerable.”
Comme d’autres organismes du quartier, l: Like other organizations in the neighbourhood, the Forum jeunesse submitted several funding requests under the<l1> Programme québécois de lutte contre la criminalité</l1> (PQLC). Without success. “We meet the criteria, we start from the needs of the young people… but apparently, that’s not what the government wants.”
Son projet, intitulé « Parcours trajecto: His project, called “Parcours trajectoires,” proposed meetings between young people and former inmates so that the youth could reflect on the consequences of certain life choices. “These are magical encounters. The kids understand which paths to avoid.”
Sur une dizaine de projets déposés par l: Of about ten projects submitted by Saint-Michel organizations under the program’s prevention component, only one was funded, according to information shared at a meeting held in March by the Comité de prévention urbaine (CPU), led by the neighbourhood roundtable Vivre Saint-Michel en santé (VSMS). It is a figure that is circulating, and it is fuelling frustration. Participants spoke of ever-growing needs in crime prevention, especially among young people. Unfortunately, those needs have not been quantified, laments Ingrid Fanéus-Lefebvre, the coordination officer in charge of safety and education files at the VSMS roundtable, who says that this measurement work “will in fact be part of the project submission for the grant application.”

Sollicité par <em>La Converse</em> pour: Asked by La Converse to explain all these rejections, especially of those submitted in a neighbourhood where youth crime is a significant issue, the Ministère de la Sécurité publique, through its communications branch, merely pointed us to “useful” links, explaining that “all the eligibility criteria are set out in the online program standards document and were addressed during the two information sessions open to the public.”
<strong>Même le SPVM plaide pour un fina: Even the SPVM is pleading for sustainable funding
Pour Mohamed Mimoun, le problème est str: For Mohamed Mimoun, the problem is structural: “Without core funding, we depend on projects. And if the projects don’t get approved… we close.”
Le financement à la mission est plus sta: Core funding is more stable and ensures a certain continuity. It would pay for rent, fixed costs and a minimum of staff. Without it, organizations chase after projects to survive, which is the case for several of them in the neighbourhood.
« On n’a plus de financement à la missio: “We no longer have core funding. Organizations go from one project to the next,” explains Ingrid Fanéus-Lefebvre. “Yet a social project takes time. Two years is often the time needed to get it established,” she says.
Subissant l’instabilité du financement,: Weighed down by unstable funding, the services these organizations offer suffer greatly: “Projects end, bonds are broken,” notes the coordination officer. “Young people get involved… then the funding stops, and they find themselves facing nothing.”
Alors qu’Ingrid Fanéus-Lefebvre insiste: While Ingrid Fanéus-Lefebvre stresses the importance of trust built over time, SPVM chief Fady Dagher points out that “the street outreach worker […] is there permanently, for years.” Invited onto a 98.5 FM radio show, Mr. Dagher acknowledged that the community sector strike directly affects the police, citing concrete repercussions for prevention work with young people.
D’ailleurs, certains aspects du plan de: Moreover, some aspects of the plan to fight discrimination and racism, launched last week by the SPVM, rely on “strong partnerships with community and institutional organizations on strategies of proximity with citizens.”
À ses yeux, ces intervenants jouent un r: In his view, these workers play a role that the police cannot fill: “The one who has a connection with that young person […] is the street outreach worker, the social worker.” Conversely, he acknowledges, the young person “doesn’t want to talk to the police, he distrusts them.” That is why he is pleading for “more regular” and “sustainable” funding for the community sector.
À Saint-Michel, les discussions au sein: In Saint-Michel, discussions within the CPU reflect exhaustion. Organizations describe repeated funding refusals, increased competition between projects, and attempts at “patching things together” to keep services going. “Lots of requests, little money,” sums up Ingrid Fanéus-Lefebvre. “And complex calls for projects, sometimes hard to adapt to the reality on the ground.” With no alternative, some are considering turning to funding components less suited to prevention. Thus, the organizations brought together in the Comité de prévention urbaine (CPU) are turning to other facets of the program, even though they are not strictly speaking intended for prevention projects.
La complainte du CPU s’inscrit dans un c: The CPU’s complaint is part of a broader context, that of the<l1> Le communautaire à boutte</l1> movement, which denounces the chronic underfunding of community organizations and the precarious working conditions of workers in the sector. The problem is not new, but the demands remain relevant.
Dans plusieurs régions du Québec, des se: In several regions of Quebec, services are running at reduced capacity or have been suspended during strike days, which took place between March 23 and April 2. A rally in front of Quebec’s National Assembly is planned for Thursday, April 2.
Il faut savoir que le gouvernement affir: It should be noted that the government says it has increased the budgets granted to Quebec community organizations, which reach <l1>$2.2 billion in 2026</l1>. An envelope that would have doubled since the CAQ came to power. The most recent <l2>report on government financial support for the community sector</l2>, however, dates from 2023-204, as we confirmed with the Ministère de l’Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale.
Une partie du décalage tient à la manièr: Part of the gap comes down to how the amounts are presented. “The funding that has been announced […] is spread over five years. It’s not new money,” explains Émilie Marchand, communications manager for the Le communautaire à boutte movement. According to her, the amounts put forward by Quebec seem large but change in scale once broken down: “When you bring it down to one year, it comes to $20 million. Then, for 3,500 groups, that comes to $6,000 a year per group.”
Des sommes jugées insuffisantes sur le t: Sums deemed insufficient on the ground, where some organizations don’t even get indexation. “It looks big in absolute terms, […] but in reality, it’s not that much,” she adds. A similar reading is offered by the Réseau québécois de l’action communautaire autonome, which recently detailed these gaps in an <l1>interview with Radio-Canada</l1>.
Interrogée sur la suite du mouvement, la: Asked about what comes next for the movement, the communications manager says the mobilization will not run out of steam. “Le Communautaire à boutte is definitely not going to stop after April 2,” she says, citing the aim of obtaining “a negotiating table with the next head of the Quebec government.” While the details remain to be worked out, one thing is already clear: “You’re going to be hearing about Le Communautaire à boutte for a long time, until the elections.” The movement’s leaders intend to make themselves heard during the election campaign and to keep up the pressure “until we get clear commitments.” Buoyed, she says, by “the public’s support,” the groups plan to “mobilize even more” in the coming months.
Dans une modeste salle de Saint-Michel,: In a modest hall in Saint-Michel, about a hundred people are attending a boxing gala on Saturday, March 28, organized by the organization Ness Martial, which offers a sports-study program to fight school dropout. In the ring, young people go from one friendly bout to the next. In the stands, parents offer encouragement. For board member Grégory Élie, the goal is twofold: “Celebrate the young people… and go after funding.”
Sa notoriété, l’organisme l’a bâtie depu: The organization has built its reputation over the years on the concrete results it has achieved with young people. That is what Billy Barbier, a Saint-Michel resident, confirms. In the crowd, he watches his daughter, who does kickboxing and is stepping into the ring tonight. “It helps her blossom. To gain confidence,” he explains.
Au-delà du sport, l’organisme agit aussi: Beyond sport, the organization also works upstream, on other levers. As a fire safety inspector and a parent, Billy Barbier has been there to present his profession to the young people. “There are people who come regularly to talk about what they do for a living. It lets the kids see different options,” he explains.
Ces rencontres, poursuit-il, jouent un r: These encounters, he continues, play a quiet but structuring role by offering accessible role models with whom teenagers can identify. “They see people who look like them, who work. It shows them it’s possible.”
Mais il s’inquiète des coupes. « Ça fait: But he is worried about the cuts. “It’s heartbreaking. These are things that should be funded.” In truth, some services have already disappeared. “We used to offer French-language classes. They were cut,” Mr. Élie warns. Two positions have indeed been eliminated, and “it’s not just the employees who are affected – it’s the next generation!” he cautions.
D’un quartier à l’autre, les constats se: From one neighbourhood to another, the findings are similar. Organizations are losing staff, cutting services, struggling to keep their premises; youth workers are paying for activities out of their own pockets and juggling limited resources; and young people are looking for bearings and oscillating between support and the street.
Pour les acteurs du terrain, l’enjeu dép: For those working on the ground, the issue goes beyond the organizations themselves. “The community sector is the social safety net,” insists Mohamed Mimoun. “During the pandemic, we’re the ones who supported the most vulnerable.” Today, that net is becoming more fragile.
Et dans les quartiers, les effets de cet: And in the neighbourhoods, the effects of this weakening are measured less in figures than in absences: one fewer youth worker, a closed door, a cancelled activity. So many small withdrawals that, added together, reshape daily life.
